sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in Kitsap County, WA?
sections.html:
The Kitsap County Treasurer collects property tax, and the Kitsap County Assessor sets the value the bill is built on. Both offices work from the Administration Building at 619 Division Street in Port Orchard, and both answer at (360) 337-5777.

The split matters when you sell. Questions about payments, due dates, refunds, delinquent years, excise tax and foreclosure go to the Treasurer. Questions about assessed value, appeals, levy rates and relief programs go to the Assessor. The Treasurer's FAQ page states the same division, and its Parcel Details site shows any tax statement and payment history by account number or address.

Mail payments go to the Kitsap County Treasurer, PO Box 169, Port Orchard WA 98366-0169. The counter at 619 Division Street is open Monday through Friday, 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

sections.h2: What should a Kitsap County seller know about the county itself?
sections.html:
Kitsap County is a peninsula county on Puget Sound, and your tax bill reflects a place with a lot of shoreline and a lot of commuters. The county was formed on January 16, 1857, and it covers the Kitsap Peninsula plus Bainbridge Island. The shoreline runs about 250 miles, and by land area the county is the fourth smallest in the state.

The incorporated cities are Bainbridge Island, Bremerton, Poulsbo and the county seat, Port Orchard. The part north of Silverdale is called North Kitsap and the part south of Bremerton is South Kitsap. Washington State Ferries and Kitsap Transit connect the county to Seattle and Edmonds.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts for Kitsap County give a sense of the market a buyer sees:

  • Population estimate for July 1, 2025: 283,374, up 2.8% from the April 2020 base.
  • Land area: 395.10 square miles, or 697.6 people per square mile in 2020.
  • Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020-2024: 70.1%.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020-2024: $555,100.
  • Median household income, 2020-2024: $104,158.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 1,780.

sections.h2: When are Kitsap County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Kitsap County property taxes are due in two halves: the first by April 30 and the second by October 31. If your total bill is $50 or less, the whole amount is due April 30. The Treasurer mails statements in February, and the due dates come from RCW 84.56.020.

Payment counts as on time if it is postmarked by the due date. The Treasurer suggests handing a letter to the post office clerk on the last day. A bank bill-pay service may mail a paper check, so set it up well ahead. The 2026 second-half date has already passed, so any unpaid balance on a parcel you plan to sell is now delinquent.

If a lender pays your taxes from escrow, the county does not send the lender a copy of your statement. The lender downloads account data from the county site, and the Treasurer tells owners to read escrow statements closely, especially after buying or refinancing.

sections.h2: What does a late payment cost in Kitsap County?
sections.html:
Late tax in Kitsap County accrues interest every month, and the rate depends on the type of property. For a home with four or fewer units, including a manufactured home, interest is 0.75% per month on the full principal balance, with no penalty. Non-residential property and residential property with more than four units pays 1% per month plus a 3% penalty on June 1 and an 8% penalty on December 1.

The Treasurer says there is no good-cause waiver, and not receiving a statement does not erase interest. The listed exceptions are narrow:

  • The county made an error and never sent the notice.
  • One missed payment on a personal residence after the death of a spouse, or of a parent or stepparent, if the Treasurer hears about it within 60 days of the due date and receives a death certificate.
  • An underpayment caused by an apparent taxpayer error, paid within 30 days of notice.
  • Military owners stationed abroad during an armed conflict.

You can pay the current year without clearing older years, but a tax year that reaches three years late can be sent to foreclosure.

sections.h2: How do I appeal my Kitsap County assessed value?
sections.html:
File a petition with the Kitsap County Board of Equalization. The deadline is July 1 of the assessment year or 60 days after the date on your value change notice, whichever is later. Kitsap uses the 60-day option that state law allows counties to adopt under RCW 84.40.038.

For the 2026 assessment year, the Assessor mailed notices on June 26, 2026, and the Board set August 31, 2026 as the last day, so that window has closed. Notices for the next assessment year should arrive in 2027, and the new deadline will print on that notice. The Board's page lays out the process:

  • There is no filing fee, and each parcel needs its own petition with a copy of the notice attached.
  • The only question is market value on the valuation date, January 1 of the assessment year.
  • Useful evidence includes comparable sales close to that date, repair estimates, easement deeds, appraisals and photographs.
  • Hearings run Tuesdays and Wednesdays, 9:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., on the fourth floor of the Administration Building or by phone.
  • Decisions usually arrive within two weeks, and state law allows 45 days.

The Assessor is presumed correct, so the burden of proof sits with you. If you disagree with the Board's decision, an appeal to the State Board of Tax Appeals must be filed within 30 days of the mailing date. Call the Board at 360-337-4424.

sections.h2: Which Kitsap County relief programs matter when you are selling?
sections.html:
The Assessor manages six programs, and a few of them change what you owe at sale. The ones listed on the Treasurer's FAQ are the senior and disabled persons exemption and deferral, the limited-income homeowner deferral, current use for farm, open space and forest land, the residential improvement exemption, the destroyed property exemption, and nonprofit exemptions.

The senior and disabled exemption under RCW 84.36.381 is open to owners who are at least 61 years old, retired because of a disability, or a veteran receiving VA compensation at the qualifying rating. It is tied to a principal residence you own, and the claimant can carry the exemption to a replacement home after a sale. Income limits and the share of value exempted change with the 2026 legislation that applies to taxes payable in 2027, so ask the Assessor for the current figures before you count on a number.

sections.h2: How does the real estate excise tax work on a Kitsap County sale?
sections.html:
The seller owes real estate excise tax, and it must be paid before the deed can be recorded. Kitsap County's local portion is 0.50%, and the state portion is graduated. Payment is due within 30 days of the date on the conveying document, and a $5 state technology fee applies. The Treasurer collects it at the Port Orchard counter by cash or check, and card payments carry fees.

Both parties sign a Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit. Since August 1, 2023, Kitsap County also requires that affidavit when it processes a Lack of Probate Affidavit, which matters for inherited homes. For sales that close on or after January 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue lists these state rates by slice of the selling price:

Portion of selling priceState REET rate
Up to $551,0001.1%
$551,001 to $1,551,0001.28%
$1,551,001 to $3,051,0002.75%
Above $3,051,0003.0%

Source: Washington Department of Revenue. Agricultural and timberland keeps a flat 1.28% state rate, and the local rate is added on top. Closings earlier than 2027 use the previous thresholds, so confirm the figure with the Treasurer or your escrow officer.

sections.h2: What happens if Kitsap County property taxes stay unpaid?
sections.html:
Once a tax year is three years late, the Treasurer begins foreclosure under chapter 84.64 RCW. As the Treasurer explains it, the full 2023 year and earlier were the at-risk years as of January 2026, and paying only those years by April 30 stops the process.

The county files foreclosure in May and serves every party with a recorded interest by certified mail, and a notice is published in the local paper. Until close of business on the last business day before the sale, the owner or any recorded interest holder can redeem by paying all taxes, interest, penalties and costs in certified funds. Personal checks are refused. After the sale, prior owners lose their rights, except minors and people a court has found incompetent, who have three years to redeem.

The Treasurer's calendar lists a tax foreclosure auction for January 26, 2027 at publicsurplus.com, with January 25, 2027 as the last day to redeem. If older years are delinquent on a home you own, a sale before foreclosure is filed is still an option.

faqs.q: Who do I call about property tax in Kitsap County?
faqs.a: Call (360) 337-5777. That number reaches both the Treasurer, for payments, due dates and foreclosure, and the Assessor, for values, appeals and relief programs.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Kitsap County house if property taxes are behind?
faqs.a: Yes. A tax year has to be three years late before foreclosure begins, so a sale before then can clear the balance. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure and give it to your escrow officer.

faqs.q: Does Kitsap County waive late interest?
faqs.a: Rarely. The Treasurer says there is no good-cause waiver, and the exceptions are limited to county error, one missed payment after a close family death, a small taxpayer payment error cured within 30 days, and military owners abroad in an armed conflict.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Kitsap County assessment?
faqs.a: You have until July 1 or 60 days after the date on the value change notice, whichever is later. The 2026 deadline was August 31, 2026, so file within the window printed on the next notice.

faqs.q: Who pays the excise tax when a Kitsap County home sells?
faqs.a: The seller pays it. It is due within 30 days of the date on the deed or other conveying document, and it must be paid before the document can be recorded.
